metadata.title: The Tide Keeps It
metadata.premise: A smuggler's lugger has broken her back on the Whistling Bar outside the fishing port of Saltmere Hollow, and the crew hiding beneath the docks cannot agree whether the crime is the drowned captain, the false lamp that killed him, or the cargo still waiting for high water.
metadata.narrationVoice: Second person, present tense; a wry harbor-pilot's voice, salt-dry and unhurried, fond of tide-times and other people's ledgers.

contentLimits.note: Saltmere's dock children appear as lookouts and gossips only; violence toward them happens nowhere on the page.

beats.title: Saltmere Hollow, Slack Water
beats.prose: Saltmere Hollow is a town built on stilts and stubbornness: a mile of black pilings, a fish-market that never quite dries, and a wreck-bell tolling from the sea wall. Two nights ago the lugger Tern's Widow put her keel through the Whistling Bar with all lamps burning and a captain named Maevar Tull locked in his own cabin. Her crew came ashore. Her cargo did not. Gulls are working something out past the surf, and every door on the quay is open a hand's width, listening.
beats.readAloud: The bell tolls once for a wreck and twice for a body. Since dawn it has tolled once, over and over, as if the town cannot bring itself to finish the sentence.

options.label: Follow the wreck-bell's crowd into the Split Keel, where the survivors are drinking.
Present yourselves at the tide-market office and ask the harbormistress for the salvage record.
Hire a dory from a one-eyed girl's grandfather and row out to the Bar before the flood.

beats.title: The Split Keel
beats.prose: The tavern leans over the water like a man being sick. Inside, four of the Tern's Widow's crew sit apart from each other on purpose. The youngest, a deckhand named Pell Ashgrove, has a bandaged ear and keeps counting the drowned on his fingers, getting a different number each time. A woman with a quartermaster's brass whistle — Nessa Crale — watches you from the settle and says nothing. The bosun's chair is empty; Ottrick Vane, they say, has gone to the shrine to argue with a god.
beats.readAloud: "Lamps," Pell says, to no one. "We had the channel lamps dead ahead. Steady as a church. And the bar was where the channel should have been."

options.label: Buy Pell a drink and coax the whole night out of him, lamp by lamp.
Take Pell's mumbled directions to the grate beneath the fish-stalls.
Leave the crew to their silence and put the questions to the harbormistress instead.

beats.title: The Tide-Market Office
beats.prose: Harbormistress Idony Sceave keeps her office above the weigh-scales, warm as a held breath. She is courteous, quick, and pours you tea before you ask a question. The salvage ledger lies open on her desk — too open, the way a thing is open when it has been arranged. Beneath the window, a chandler's crate stamped BRANNOC & SLADE sits with its lid prised and its straw disturbed.
beats.readAloud: "A wreck is bookkeeping, friends," Sceave says. "Tull was drunk, the bar moved, the sea took its tithe. I have three widows to pay and no appetite for stories."

options.label: Read the salvage ledger sideways while she talks about widows.
Ask why a sober captain would be locked inside his own cabin.
Excuse yourselves, then take the weigh-house back stairs down into the underwharf.

beats.title: The Whistling Bar
beats.prose: At slack water the Whistling Bar shows itself: a long spine of shingle that hums when the swell crosses it. The Tern's Widow lies broken across it in two pieces, her mast down and pointing accusingly at the town. Her hold is scoured empty — swept clean by hands, not by sea; the drag-marks go landward. Aft, the cabin door is still shut, and there is a fresh iron staple driven through the frame from the outside.
beats.readAloud: The bar whistles under your boots. Half a mile off, on the shingle's high point, someone has built a neat little cairn of stones — and neat is the last word this coast deserves.

options.label: Dive the flooded cabin and bring up Maevar Tull's soaked log.
Walk the shingle to the cairn where something was burning two nights ago.
Follow the cask-drag marks back landward to the underdock grate.

beats.title: The False Lamp
beats.prose: The cairn is knee-high and wind-braced, with a scorched flat stone on top and a hooded ship's lantern wedged in its lee, wick trimmed, reservoir still slick with good oil. Two nights of rain have not washed away the tally-marks scratched into the flat stone: three short strokes, then one long. Whoever sat here sat a while, and lit this thing at exactly the hour a lugger running the coast would look landward for the channel pair.
beats.readAloud: Stand where the lamp stood, and look out. From here — and only from here — a false light and the true harbor light line up like an honest pair of eyes. Sail between them and you sail onto the Bar.

options.label: Reconstruct the sight-lines: prove the lamp was a lure, not a beacon.
Pry the lantern's brass plate for the chandler's mark and the office it was issued to.
Leave the lamp where it stands. Lamps don't pay; cargo does.

beats.title: Under the Fish-Stalls
beats.prose: The underwharf is a drowned cathedral: rank on rank of tarred pilings, walkways of stolen planking, and the whole ceiling a floor, with market voices and boot-thumps passing overhead. Rope ladders climb to hammock lofts slung between beams. Somewhere ahead, water slaps in a low gallery, and something that isn't water moves in it. Fresh cask-drag scars shine on the mud, heading deeper toward the sea wall.
beats.readAloud: Low tide gives you two hours of dry knees. The wrack-line on the pilings is at your throat.

options.label: Wade the low gallery while the tide is out and the shortcut exists.
Climb the piling ladders to the crew's hammock loft, where the arguing is loudest.
Follow the cask-drag marks quietly, all the way in.

beats.title: The Low Gallery
beats.prose: The gallery narrows to a crawl of slime and shell, and the flood arrives early — it always arrives early. Wharf rats the size of terriers come boiling off the ledges ahead of the water, and behind them, two of Crale's tide-watchers with boat-hooks and no interest in your names. Nobody wins an argument in a rising tunnel. You only get out of it.
beats.readAloud: Water at your shins. Water at your knees. Somewhere ahead, a grating of light — go, go, go.

beats.title: The Salt-Hold
beats.prose: Beyond the gallery, in a chamber dug into the sea wall itself, the cargo of the Tern's Widow is stacked above the wrack-line: forty lead casks, seams sealed with pitch, each stencilled with a gull and the word HOLLOW. Inside is grey salt, fine as flour and faintly warm. It does not preserve fish. Butchers inland pay hard coin because meat packed in it does not rot — does not rot at all, ever, and sometimes twitches. The chalk tally on the wall says thirty-nine were landed. Someone has already sold one.
beats.readAloud: Put a pinch on your tongue and the taste is old copper and low tide. Your own hand feels, for a heartbeat, like something you are only borrowing.

options.label: Crack a seal and work out precisely what the grey salt is for.
Douse your lights and wait in the dark for whoever comes for the casks.
Sling one cask on a pole and carry the evidence up into daylight.

beats.title: Two Whistles, One Crew
beats.prose: In the hammock loft the Underwharf tears itself in half in front of you. Quartermaster Nessa Crale wants the casks moved on tonight's high water: the crew is owed, the widows are owed, and a dead captain buys nobody bread. Bosun Ottrick Vane wants the lamp-setter named and hung, and he will burn the cargo to make the town look at it. Pell Ashgrove sits between them with his fingers going, still counting the drowned. Both leaders turn to you at once. The tide gives you about an hour.
beats.readAloud: "Cargo," says Crale. "Captain," says Vane. "Both," says Pell, very quietly, and neither of them hears him.

options.label: Side with Bosun Vane: the drowned man first, and let the cargo wait.
Side with Quartermaster Crale: move the casks on the flood and settle debts.
Refuse both whistles and try to hold the middle of the loft.

beats.title: Crale's Flood Crew
beats.prose: Crale does not shout. She blows her brass whistle twice, and the underwharf answers with boat-hooks and cudgels: her flood crew, come to shift casks and any obstacle between the casks and the water. You do not have to beat them. You only have to still be standing when the sea comes up over the ledge and ends the shift for everybody.
beats.readAloud: "Nothing personal," Crale calls over the din. "Everything's personal at low water. Hold on till the flood and we'll talk like people."

beats.title: Sceave's Parlour
beats.prose: Idony Sceave receives you again, and this time she does not pour tea. Her enforcer, Grishen Awl, stands at the shutters with his thumbs in his belt and the harbor at his back. On the sideboard: a hooded lantern of the same pattern as the one on the Bar, its brass plate freshly unscrewed. Sceave took a bribe to wreck a ship in shallow water where the cargo could be lifted, and she nailed a staple through a captain's door so he would not swim ashore to complain.
beats.readAloud: "Say it plainly, if you're going to," Sceave says. "This town has been drowning men for profit since before it had a name. I merely kept the accounts tidy."

options.label: Lay the evidence on her desk and name her before her own clerks.
Bargain instead: her silence bought with a share of the grey salt.
Say nothing, then slip into her private wharf-shed while she answers the tide-bell.

beats.title: Grishen Awl Shuts the Shutters
beats.prose: Sceave sighs like a woman rained on, and Grishen Awl closes the shutters. He has two weigh-house bruisers and a cutlass he keeps for ledger disputes; the room smells of tallow and fish-oil and the coming argument. Put Awl down and the rest will remember they are paid by the hour, not by the wound.
beats.readAloud: "Nobody dies in the customs house," Awl says, drawing. "That's what the harbor's for."

beats.title: High Water
beats.prose: The flood comes in fast under Saltmere Hollow, and everything that has been argued all day gets decided in twenty minutes of black water. Crale's crew has slings rigged to walk the casks out to a waiting hoy. Vane stands on the ledge with a lit lamp and a broached cask of pitch. Sceave's boat is loaded and pointed at the channel. Above your heads the market is closing, and the wreck-bell is still tolling once, once, once.
beats.readAloud: The sea comes up through the planks like something remembering the shape of a room. Choose now, and the tide will do the rest — it always does the rest.

options.label: Stave the casks and let the flood carry the grey salt out past the Bar forever.
Ring the wreck-bell twice and hand the false lamp to the whole assembled fleet.
Take your share of the water-borne coin and let Saltmere keep its silence.

beats.title: Two Strokes of the Bell
beats.prose: Two strokes of the wreck-bell means a body, and Saltmere Hollow has never learned to ignore it. Boats come off their moorings by lamplight; the fish-market becomes a court with the false lantern set on the weigh-scales as its only witness. Idony Sceave is taken on her own quay with the tide-market ledger still under her arm, and the iron staple from Maevar Tull's cabin door is passed hand to hand until nobody can pretend it was weather. Ottrick Vane reads the drowned list aloud and gets the number right. Nessa Crale spits, hands over the sling-ropes, and takes the widows' share instead of the buyers' — she will not thank you, but she will drink with you. The grey salt goes into the sea wall under lock and quicklime, and Pell Ashgrove stops counting on his fingers. The bell is quiet by morning. The port is poorer, and looks it, and stands.
beats.readAloud: "Wreck once," says the old bellman, and hauls again. "Body twice. That's the whole law of this coast, and I've waited forty years to use the second half."

beats.title: Thirty-Nine Casks and a Clean Bar
beats.prose: You go along the ledge staving lids as the flood takes your waist, and the grey salt goes out through the underwharf in a pale, warm smoke that the sea swallows without comment. Forty thousand in cargo becomes a stain on the shingle. Crale screams at you from the hoy until she runs out of words, then rows away with an empty hold and a crew who will follow her again next season, because she is good at this and there will be other seasons. Idony Sceave keeps her office; without the cargo there is no case, only a lamp on a cairn and a bosun's grudge. But nothing inland gets packed in Saltmere's grey salt this year, and nothing packed in it comes back twitching. Ottrick Vane takes the staple from Tull's door and nails it above the Split Keel's hearth, where the town has to look at it while it drinks.
beats.readAloud: The last cask goes over and the whistling of the Bar changes pitch, just slightly, the way a held note does when someone finally lets go.

beats.title: The Tide Keeps It
beats.prose: However you come to it — dragged senseless out of a flooding gallery by strangers who take your purse for the trouble, or walking off the ledge dry-shod with Crale's coin heavy in your coat — the ending is the same shape. The hoy clears the Bar on the top of the tide. Thirty-nine casks go inland to buyers who ask no questions of a preservative that works too well. Idony Sceave pays three widows out of the salvage fund and is commended for her diligence. Ottrick Vane is found a month later, face-down and sober, and the bell tolls once for him too, because once is cheaper. Pell Ashgrove signs on with another crew and never says the word lamp again. Somewhere inland, in a butcher's cold-room, meat packed in grey salt shifts on its hook. Saltmere Hollow keeps whistling. The tide keeps what it took, and the town lets it.
beats.readAloud: The wreck-bell tolls once. Just once. In this port, that is not an accident; it is a policy.

encounters.title: Grishen Awl and the Weigh-House Men
